notes: RF: Family Resources Survey 2024-25, GB, with the IPPR tax-benefit model.
Eligibility shares are for the income test alone; passporting is separate.
Passporting uses modelled receipt with the datasets' take-up draws; RF uses receipt reported in the FRS, which is also shown.

Family-type rows count benefit units wherever they live, as RF's Figure 4 does, on two bases. RF's basis is the difference between the two income-test series, without netting out passporting, which is what RF's 490,000 and 780,000 measure. The policy count nets it out: units whose household is eligible under only one of the two options, since passported households are eligible under both. RF does not publish it.
Deciles rank people by equivalised household income after housing costs, the HBAI convention; RF does not say which weighting it uses. Rows marked 'deciles of households' rank households instead.

The family-type counts run above RF's. Part of the gap is the passporting basis (modelled rather than reported receipt). Most of the pensioner gap on Microcosm is household composition: it has more multi-family households than the Enhanced FRS, and a pensioner living with an adult child in work passes the individual test and can fail the household one.

£2bn averages divide £2bn among all recipients (passported or passing the test), and separately among households passing the income test only, which is closer to how RF's averages appear to be costed. For the tiered option, RF does not say which tier passported households get; the all-recipient figure places them in the top tier.

external_sources.quantity: RF targeted energy discount: share of households eligible under a £24,000 highest-individual-income threshold (plus means-tested benefit passporting)
external_sources.title: Billing me softly (10 August 2026)
external_sources.note: All values 'around'. The report states 75% coverage of the poorest four deciles of equivalised AHC income; the press release (https://www.resolutionfoundation.org/press-releases/government-must-be-ready-to-provide-targeted-energy-support-if-further-price-spikes-cause-more-families-to-struggle-this-winter/) states 83% of the poorest fifth. These are different populations, not a contradiction. Eligibility is tested on taxable income, while deciles use HBAI AHC income, so coverage is below 100% even in the poorest decile. The alternative total household income test (under £30,000, OECD BHC-equivalised) also reaches about 40% of households. Source data: RF analysis of the FRS, GB, 2024-25.

external_sources.quantity: RF targeted energy discount: scheme cost and average discount per eligible household
external_sources.title: Billing me softly (10 August 2026)
external_sources.note: Delivered as a unit-rate discount on gas and electricity, so the value varies with consumption. £175 is the average over eligible households. The tiered amounts are 'around' values within the same £2bn envelope. RF says the cost should be met from public funds, not a bill levy. Implied eligible households at £2bn / £175 is about 11.4 million (my derivation, not stated by RF).

external_sources.title: Billing me softly (10 August 2026)
external_sources.note: Passporting reach is stated as 'around a quarter' of British households. The VAT figure (about £45 a year) matches Ofgem's statement for the Oct-Dec 2026 cap. Of the 490,000 working-age couples with children who lose out, 71% are in the poorest fifth; of the 780,000 pensioner households who gain, 81% (630,000) are in decile five or above. Also stated: more than 15% of second-quintile households could not afford to keep their home warm in 2022-23. The press release says 'second income quartile', but the report says quintile.
